headline: The consumer cracked: retail sales -0.6% and sentiment to 51.0 with inflation expectations still rising — and a third tanker was hit ahead of Monday's Iran deadline
client_frame:
Friday delivered the week's most important data, and it was not good. **July retail sales fell 0.6% month-over-month against +0.1% expected** — the largest monthly decline in 14 months and the first outright drop in nine. The control group that feeds GDP fell **0.4%** versus +0.3% expected, its worst reading since January 2025, and June was revised down. The weakness was broad rather than a gasoline artifact: online retail −2.2%, autos −1.8%, electronics −0.5%. Set against July payrolls of **−23,000**, the read is a consumer genuinely weakening, not merely normalizing.

An hour and a half later, **Michigan sentiment came in at 51.0 against 55.2 in July** and roughly 54.5 expected — and the internals were worse than the headline. Current conditions fell to 51.8, expectations to 50.6, and **one-year inflation expectations rose to 4.3% from 4.2%**, well above the 3.4% reading in February before the Iran conflict. Only 8% of consumers now expect their income to outpace inflation. That combination — falling activity with rising inflation expectations — is the uncomfortable one, and it is why this is not a straightforward case for the Fed to cut into weakness.

Markets took it calmly. The S&P slipped **0.17% to 7,785.76**, giving back a fraction of Thursday's record close of 7,798.99, so **Thursday's high remains the record and Friday did not set a new one**. The Nasdaq 100 eased 0.13% and the Dow 0.20%, while the Russell 2000 actually rose 0.51% — an odd small-cap divergence on a weak-consumer day. VIX fell to 14.25. **The bond market disagreed with the growth read**: the 10-year rose about 5.5bp to 4.696%, extending the message from the week's two poorly-received auctions rather than rallying on soft data. On the week the S&P added 0.36% and the Nasdaq 100 1.09%, while the Dow lost 0.56%.

One correction worth making explicitly. Several wires reported that September hike odds fell to about 30.6% after the data. **Our direct CME pull for the 8/14 cohort shows hold 66.9% / hike 33.1%** — barely changed from Thursday's 34.1%. The direction is right but the magnitude in the press coverage is overstated; the market did not meaningfully reprice on Friday's misses. The four-day path is 49.6% hike (8/10) → 40.6% → 34.1% → **33.1%**.

The week ahead is unusually loaded. **Monday is the reported expiry of the 60-day window** in June's interim US-Iran memorandum, and there is still no confirmed extension — a third ADNOC-operated tanker was struck Friday evening. **Wednesday brings Canada's 50% tariffs** at 12:01am and **July FOMC minutes** at 2pm. And five major retailers report between Tuesday and Thursday — Home Depot, Target, Lowe's, TJX and Walmart — which is the best possible follow-up to a bad retail sales print. Jackson Hole is the week after, August 27–29, with Warsh's first keynote as Chair expected on the 28th.

geo_headlines: **MONDAY IS THE DEADLINE.** The 60-day window in June's interim US-Iran memorandum reportedly expires August 17 with **no confirmed extension**. A **third ADNOC-operated tanker was attacked Friday evening**, the third in a week; UKMTO confirmed a bulk carrier struck by an unknown projectile. Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Baqaei: 'We are not currently negotiating with the United States.' The Anadolu report of an agreement in principle to extend remains **uncorroborated and directly contradicted** by Iranian officials via Reuters.

**Quiet diplomacy is running through Europe:** Secretary Rubio met Austria's foreign minister and called Greece's, and both then spoke with Iran's FM Araghchi on Thursday. Austria has offered to host talks. Iran frames the contacts as being about 'future management of the Strait of Hormuz', not a bilateral deal.

**Oil finished the week up 5–6%** — WTI $82.40 and Brent $88.52 — after Defense Secretary Hegseth threatened an 'indefinite' naval blockade of Iranian ports. Both benchmarks had dipped roughly 2% Thursday before reversing.

**Canada's 50% Section 338 tariffs** on ~$20B of goods hit at 12:01am ET **Wednesday**, with **no USMCA exemption** unlike prior rounds. Canada's chief negotiator Janice Charette said Friday there is 'a significant amount of work to do'; talks run through the weekend. The sticking point is US insistence on keeping some auto tariffs even inside a deal.

**Five major retailers report Tue–Thu:** Home Depot (Tue BO), Target, Lowe's and TJX (Wed BO), Walmart (Thu BO), plus Deere Thursday. The most direct consumer read available after Friday's miss. Home Depot reports with CEO Ted Decker on medical leave.

**July FOMC minutes land Wednesday 2pm** — the only scheduled Fed communication of the week. **No Board speeches are on the calendar August 17–21**, which likely means officials are holding fire until Jackson Hole.

**Jackson Hole is August 27–29**, not this week — theme 'Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy'. Chair Warsh's first keynote as Chair is expected Friday the 28th, 19 days before the September decision.

**Also on deck:** Empire State manufacturing and NAHB Monday; import/export prices, housing starts and industrial production Tuesday; jobless claims, Philly Fed and leading indicators Thursday; flash PMIs and monthly options expiration Friday.
